title: The services page a restaurant group actually needs
metaTitle: The services page a restaurant group needs
excerpt: Name what a guest can actually do: eat here, book a table, hold a private dinner. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. Vague tiles do not help.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, a street where someone is already choosing which door to walk through.
caption: A street full of doors. The page should say which one serves dinner. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a restaurant group have a page called Services?
faqs.answer: Only if that is a word your guests use. Most of them are looking for dinner, a specific restaurant, private dining, or a group booking. Use those words as the headings. The page still has to do the job of a services page: outcome, boundary, and a way to see the menu or book.

faqs.question: What counts as an offer?
faqs.answer: A night or a room a guest can choose: dinner at a named restaurant, lunch, a private room for a known headcount, or a buyout if you sell one. Each offer needs a result, a limit, and a next step. Passion, provenance, and community are not offers.

faqs.question: Can several restaurants share one booking button?
faqs.answer: Only if the next screen makes them pick a room before they pick a time. Better: each restaurant's block has its own menu link and its own booking link, already aimed at that room. A shared button that forgets the venue creates the wrong table.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A restaurant group services page should list what a guest can actually do, in the guest's words. Someone deciding where to go tonight needs each offer to carry an outcome, a boundary, and a next step: see the menu or book a table. A grid of vague capabilities does not help them choose a door.

You may not call the page Services. Dinner, restaurants, and private dining are better headings if those are the words people already use. The job stays the same. Name the thing they can hire for an evening, and stop when the list is true.

## Guest language, not brand language

Guests do not arrive hoping to consume an experiential platform. They arrive wanting a table, a known room, or a private dinner that will not embarrass them. The headings should be those wants. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that are descriptive and concise. "Offerings" fails. "Dinner at Holt Street" passes if Holt Street is the room. "Private dining" passes if a room can be booked.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the heading summarizes the page and whether a reader can act. A tile that says "Gather" with a paragraph about memories does neither. Write the line a guest would text: "They have a private room for eighteen, and you book it by writing, not through the normal widget."

Read the current page and highlight every word you would not say at the pass. Those words are the edit. Replace them with the meal, the room, or the headcount. The brand voice can be warm. It still has to name the product.

If the group name is famous and the rooms are not, lead with the rooms. The group is the signature at the bottom. The guest is choosing a chair.

## Outcome, boundary, next step

Every block needs three parts.

The outcome is the evening they get. A table for dinner in a specific room. Lunch on weekdays. A private room with a set menu. A buyout of the whole restaurant on a dark Monday. Say the result in one sentence. "A hosted journey" is not a result.

The boundary is who it is for and who it is not. Party size. Which restaurant. How far ahead. Whether children, cakes, or speeches are welcome. A boundary is a kindness. It stops a guest from booking a romantic counter for a group of sixteen.

The next step is the menu or the booking, aimed at that offer. Dinner links to tonight's menu and the book button for that venue. Private dining links to a short note: date, headcount, which room. Do not send both through the same vague form.

Use one pattern so the page scans:

- Name of the offer, in guest words.
- The outcome in two sentences.
- The boundary in two sentences.
- Menu or book, already specific.

Then one photograph of that room or that dish. A services page without the room is a brochure. A room without the boundary is another homepage.

## What you actually sell tonight

Most groups can tell the truth with a short list. Add a line only when you want more of that business.

Dinner at each restaurant. Outcome: a booked table or a clear walk-in policy. Boundary: hours, party size the widget allows, which nights are set-menu only. Next step: menu and book for that room.

Lunch, if it is real. Outcome: a quicker meal at the spend you already show. Boundary: days, and whether the dinner room even opens. Next step: the lunch menu. Do not feature lunch on a Monday you are closed.

Private dining. Outcome: a room, a menu, a host who knows the plan. Boundary: minimum numbers, the spend or the set price, the lead time. Next step: a short inquiry, not the two-top widget.

A full buyout, only if you do it. Outcome: the restaurant, closed to the public, for a stated window. Boundary: the nights you refuse, the staff you require, the fact that this is not a large ordinary booking. Next step: a conversation with a named person.

Drop "experiences," "collaborations," and "chef's table" unless a guest can book that exact thing this month. A heading is an invitation. Do not invite a supper club you ran once.

## Why the capability grid fails

The grid shows up as four tiles: Food, People, Place, Story. It comforts the brand workshop. A guest on the sidewalk cannot tell which tile gets them dinner. They already believe you have a story. They came to see if they can sit down.

Tiles hide the boundary. Everything sounds included. The host then explains, at 7:30, that the back room is not available for twelve. That explanation belonged on the page.

Replace the grid with the offers above, even if the page gets shorter. Three true blocks beat eight abstract ones. Put the matching room under each block. The picture is the proof. The heading is the label.

Check the words against the books. If the page promises lunch and the restaurant has not served lunch since last winter, fix the page today. A services page that outruns the floor will be corrected by angry guests. Correct it yourself first.

If a partner wants the page to feel bigger, add the neighborhood and the hours, not a new abstraction. Size comes from clarity. A long adjective is not a second restaurant.

## One next step, aimed correctly

Each offer ends on menu or book, or on the private inquiry. Keep the labels boring and stable. "Menu." "Book a table." "Ask about the private room." Three labels. Not a new metaphor per restaurant.

The public widget must open on the right venue. Test it. A group with three rooms and one booking link that defaults to the flagship will silently steal parties from the other two, or dump them on a floor that cannot seat them. The link is part of the offer. Treat a wrong deep link as a wrong heading.

Hours sit in the block, as text. A guest should see that this room is dark on Monday before they hit Book. If the widget also knows that, good. The page should not depend on the widget to tell the truth.

If the list is still a fog of brand words, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) and bring the current tiles plus a week's reservations. The useful work is renaming the offers in guest language and wiring each one to the right next step. Hanabi designs and builds marketing sites where those blocks stay editable, so a closed lunch service does not live on as a poster. The call to action on your page remains the guest's menu or table, not a tour of the group.

Keep the office story off this page except as a link. Who cooks is the about page. What they can book is this one.

## Hours, place, and the block a host can edit

The offer is incomplete without the facts a host repeats. Put the address in the block, as text a guest can copy into a message. Put today's pattern of hours in the same block, not only inside the booking widget. A widget can be wrong, slow, or blocked. The sentence on the page is the promise.

Say how a walk-in is treated if you take them. "We keep a few seats at the counter after six, first come" is an offer with a boundary. Silence reads as either a welcome or a refusal, and guests will guess wrong. If a room is bookings only, say that next to Book so the word matches the door.

Name who updates the block when a service changes. A Tuesday lunch that ended should disappear the day it ends, not after the next brand meeting. The person on the floor knows first. Give them a way to change hours and the one-line description without exporting a picture. A group that waits on a designer for a closure notice will serve a wave of guests who trusted the site.

Read the blocks the way a concierge would. Could they book the right room from this page alone, without calling you? If they would still call to ask which door, the page has not listed the work in the guest's language. Add the missing noun. Cut the adjective that replaced it. Then put the menu link on that same block so the concierge, or the guest, can finish.

## Who stands in the room

A clear list still leaves a human question. Who is cooking, and who runs the floor? A guest deciding tonight may not need a biography. A guest booking a private room often does. They want a name and a reason to trust the night.

That page fails when it becomes an origin myth about the first lease. Read [how a restaurant group should write an about page](/blog/how-a-restaurant-group-should-write-an-about-page) once the offers are in guest language. The services say what can be booked. The about page says who will be there when the booking becomes a service. Write that page while the offers are still clear, before a new tile creeps back in and the guest has to guess which door serves dinner.
